title: Words & Language · Episode 3
chapters: Invented languages: from Esperanto to Klingon
Does your language shape how you think

units.t: Words & Language. Episode three.
In this episode: The world's languages, Invented languages: from Esperanto to Klingon and Does your language shape how you think.
Part one. The world's languages.
Humans speak around 7,000 languages, yet half of us speak one of just a couple of dozen.
Many of the rest, including most of Australia's own, are at risk of falling silent.
About 7,000 languages.
Linguists count roughly 7,000 living languages, including a few hundred sign languages.

The figure depends on where you draw the line between a language and a dialect, which is often as much about politics as linguistics; a famous quip says 'a language is a dialect with an army and navy'.
Languages are shared very unevenly.
More than half the world's people speak one of only about two dozen, while thousands have fewer than 10,000 speakers each.
English leads in total speakers, roughly 1.
5 billion, followed by Mandarin, Hindi and Spanish.
Mandarin has the most native speakers, then Spanish and English.
Rankings shift with how varieties are grouped, so treat lists as approximate.
Where diversity lives.
Papua New Guinea, with a relatively small population, has around 840 languages, more than any other country and over a tenth of the world's total.
Indonesia and Nigeria each have several hundred.
Rugged mountains, islands, rainforest and a long history of small, independent communities help languages multiply.
Much of Europe has relatively few.
Some languages have features English speakers find astonishing, such as tones that change meaning, or words that pack a whole sentence into one.
Languages in danger.
Around 40 per cent of the world's languages are considered endangered, usually because children are no longer learning them at home.
Pressure comes from bigger languages used in schools, jobs, government and media, and in many places from past policies that punished people for speaking their own language.
When the last speakers die, a language becomes 'sleeping' or extinct, and with it can go knowledge of local plants, animals, history, law and ways of seeing the world.
Estimates of how fast languages are being lost vary, but the trend is clear.
Australia's first languages.
When the British arrived in 1788, Australia was one of the most linguistically diverse places on Earth.
More than 250 distinct languages were spoken, with many dialects.
In the Torres Strait, Meriam Mir and Kala Lagaw Ya are traditional, and the creole Yumplatok is widely spoken.
Across the north, the creole Kriol is the first language of thousands of Aboriginal people.
Colonisation brought dispossession and, for decades, policies that discouraged or banned Aboriginal languages in missions and schools.
The 2020 National Indigenous Languages Report, based on a 2019 survey, found about 120 traditional languages still spoken, but only around 12 learned by children as a first language.
Strong ones include Warlpiri and Pitjantjatjara.
In the 2021 Census, about 77,000 people spoke an Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander language at home.
Waking languages up.
Languages no longer spoken are often called 'sleeping', not dead, because they can be woken.
Hebrew, used for centuries mainly in religious study, became an everyday language again from the late 1800s.
Māori language nests, Te Kōhanga Reo, from 1982, and Welsh revival have had real success.
In Australia, Kaurna, the language of the Adelaide Plains, is being revived partly from records made by German missionaries around 1840.
Wiradjuri, Dharug and others are taught in communities, schools and universities.
These languages belong to their communities, who decide how they are shared.
Look for programs run or endorsed by local language centres, learn the name of the Country where you live, and follow community guidance on restricted words, names or songs.
The UN has declared 2022-2032 the International Decade of Indigenous Languages.
The key idea: There are roughly 7,000 living languages, but half the world's people speak one of about two dozen.
Part two. Invented languages: from Esperanto to Klingon.
People have built entire languages from scratch, hoping to unite the world, deepen a fantasy, or just for fun.
Most failed.
A few took on lives of their own.
A very old hobby.
Constructed languages, often called conlangs, are designed by a person rather than evolving naturally in a community.
One of the earliest recorded is the Lingua Ignota, or unknown language, created by the German abbess Hildegard of Bingen in the twelfth century, with around a thousand invented words.
In the 1600s, philosophers such as John Wilkins in England tried to build perfectly logical languages, where every word's form would reveal its meaning by sorting all of reality into categories.
These schemes were brilliant and unusable.
Historians have counted hundreds of attempts.
Their makers have had three main motives: to help people from different nations communicate, to explore ideas about logic and thought, or to bring a fictional world to life.
Volapük, then Esperanto.
In 1879 Johann Martin Schleyer, a Catholic priest in southern Germany, published Volapük, an international language.
In the 1880s it spread astonishingly fast, with clubs, journals and congresses, and supporters claimed a very large following, though such numbers are hard to verify.
But Volapük was difficult, with complex grammar and words so altered from their sources that they were hard to recognise.
When reformers proposed simplifying it, Schleyer insisted on keeping control, and the movement split.
Within a few years most followers had moved to a rival.
That rival was Esperanto, published in 1887 by Ludwik Zamenhof, an eye doctor from Białystok, then part of the Russian Empire.
He believed a neutral shared language could reduce the mistrust between the Poles, Jews, Germans and Russians around him.
Spelling is phonetic and grammar has very few exceptions.
Persecuted but persistent.
Esperanto's internationalism made authoritarian regimes suspicious.
In Nazi Germany it was attacked as a Jewish conspiracy, partly because Zamenhof was Jewish, and the movement was suppressed.
In Stalin's Soviet Union, many Esperantists were arrested in the purges of the late 1930s, accused of contact with foreigners.
Zamenhof's own children were killed in the Holocaust.
Even so, the language survived, holding world congresses, publishing original literature and translations, and later thriving online.
Estimates of speakers vary enormously, from tens of thousands of fluent users to perhaps a couple of million with some knowledge.
It never became the global second language its founder hoped for.
English largely took that role, for reasons of power and economics rather than design.
Still, it remains the most successful international language ever created.
Tolkien's secret vice.
J. R. R. Tolkien was a professional philologist, an expert in the history of languages, and he invented languages from his teenage years onwards.
He called the hobby his secret vice in a 1931 lecture.
For Tolkien, the languages came before the stories.
He later explained that he built his mythology partly to give his languages a world and a history in which they could exist.
His two main Elvish languages were modelled on real ones he loved.
Quenya drew on the sounds of Finnish, while Sindarin was influenced by Welsh.
He also worked out how they had changed over thousands of years of imagined history.
That depth helps explain why Middle-earth feels so ancient: its names carry the weight of invented centuries.
Klingon and Dothraki.
In 1984 the linguist Marc Okrand developed the Klingon language for the film Star Trek III, building on a few words used earlier in the series.
He deliberately gave it unusual features to sound alien, including a basic word order of object, verb, subject, which is rare among human languages.
The Klingon Dictionary followed in 1985, and devoted fans have since translated works including Hamlet.
Later, the linguist David J. Peterson created Dothraki and High Valyrian for the television series Game of Thrones, and languages for many other productions.
These languages have consistent grammar and vocabulary, which is why fans can learn them.
Some have even appeared in mainstream language learning apps, a sign of how seriously the art is now taken.
The key idea: People have invented languages for nearly nine centuries, for logic, communication or fiction.
Part three. Does your language shape how you think.
Do Inuit really have hundreds of words for snow?
Does a language without left and right change how you see the world?
The truth is stranger and more subtle than the myths.
Whorf's big idea.
Benjamin Lee Whorf was a chemical engineer who worked for a fire insurance company in Connecticut and studied linguistics in his spare time, partly under Edward Sapir.
He noticed workers being careless near drums labelled ‘empty’ that still held explosive vapour.
The word, he suggested, was shaping their behaviour.
In the 1930s he argued that speakers of very different languages think differently.
This became the Sapir-Whorf hypothesis, though neither man stated it formally.
The strong version says language sets the limits of thought.
It is almost certainly false: babies and animals reason without words, and we keep inventing words for new ideas.
The weak version, linguistic relativity, says language nudges what you notice and remember.
Two famous myths.
Whorf claimed the Hopi language of Arizona had no words or grammar for time as we understand it.
In 1983 the linguist Ekkehart Malotki documented extensive Hopi time expressions, including words for days, seasons and units of time.
The claim that Inuit have dozens or hundreds of words for snow grew from a modest remark by the anthropologist Franz Boas, who mentioned four root words.
It swelled with each retelling until Laura Martin and Geoffrey Pullum debunked it in the 1980s.
Inuit languages build long words from many parts, so counting words misleads, and English has plenty of snow words too.
No left or right.
Some of the strongest evidence for linguistic relativity comes from Australia.
Speakers of Guugu Yimithirr, from Cape York in Queensland, do not use words like left, right, in front or behind to say where things are.
They use cardinal directions, even at small scales: there is an ant on your northern leg.
John Haviland and Stephen Levinson found that speakers kept remarkably accurate track of direction at all times, even indoors or after travelling, because their language demands it.
When people turned around and recreated arrangements of objects, such speakers preserved compass direction.
English and Dutch speakers preserved left and right.
Colour, number and time.
Russian has separate basic words for lighter blue, goluboy, and darker blue, siniy.
In a 2007 study, Russian speakers were slightly faster at telling two shades apart across that boundary, but not when they silently repeated numbers, which suggests language was involved.
The Pirahã of the Amazon have no exact number words.
In several experiments they struggled with exact quantities beyond about three, though results varied.
Number words may be a cognitive tool for exactness.
English speakers lay time out left to right, Hebrew and Arabic speakers often right to left, and Kuuk Thaayorre speakers on Cape York east to west, whichever way they face.
Aymara links the past with the front, since you can see it.
Where the debate stands.
Most researchers now accept a modest form of relativity.
Language does not trap anyone's mind, but it guides attention, makes some distinctions easier to notice and remember, and provides tools like number words.
Caution is still essential.
Some well-publicised findings, such as grammatical gender changing how people describe objects, have proved hard to replicate.
Claims linking grammar to behaviour like saving money remain contested.
Critics such as the psychologist Steven Pinker argue that thought runs on something deeper than any particular language.
Learning another language may not rewire your mind, but it can show you distinctions you never noticed.
The key idea: Language may nudge what we notice and remember, but it does not set the limits of what we can think.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. What is striking about how the world's languages are shared?
Answer. A few big languages dominate while thousands are small.
Question two. What did philosophers like John Wilkins try to build?
Answer. Logical languages where words reveal meaning.
Question three. Why is the strong version of the Sapir-Whorf idea almost certainly false?
Answer. People can think about things they have no words for.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
